steps: BENEVOLENT means well-meaning, kind, and wanting to help others.
Example: “The benevolent neighbor gave free rice to families hit by the flood.”
‘Kind’ describes the same good-hearted attitude, so it is the closest meaning.

wrong.Cruel: Cruel means wanting to hurt others. That is the opposite of benevolent.
wrong.Lazy: Lazy is about not wanting to work. It has nothing to do with kindness.
wrong.Angry: Angry describes a bad mood or temper, not a kind and helpful attitude.

0.tip: ‘Bene-’ means good (think ‘benefit’), so benevolent = good-willed, kind.

steps: FRUGAL means careful with money; spending only what is needed.
Example: “A frugal student saves part of her allowance every day.”
The question asks for the OPPOSITE. Someone who spends carelessly is ‘wasteful’.

wrong.Thrifty: Thrifty means saving money. That is a synonym (same meaning), not the opposite.
wrong.Careful: Careful is close to frugal in meaning, so it cannot be the opposite.
wrong.Modest: Modest means simple or not boastful. It is not the opposite of saving money.

1.tip: For ‘opposite’ questions, first find the meaning, then look for the word that means the reverse.

steps: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. Here there are two: ‘the manager’ and ‘the employees’, joined by ‘neither…nor’.
Rule: with ‘neither…nor’ (and ‘either…or’), the verb agrees with the subject NEARER to it.
The nearer subject is ‘employees’, which is plural, so we need a plural verb.
Correct sentence: “Neither the manager nor the employees were aware of the new policy.”

wrong.was: ‘Was’ is singular, but the nearer subject ‘employees’ is plural.
wrong.is: ‘Is’ is singular, and it is also present tense; the nearer subject ‘employees’ needs a plural verb.
wrong.has been: ‘Has’ is singular. A plural subject like ‘employees’ would need ‘have been’.

2.tip: Neither/either…nor/or: look at the subject closest to the verb and match it.

steps: Find the subject: ‘Each’ (of the applicants). The phrase ‘of the applicants’ only describes it.
‘Each’ means every single one taken one at a time, so it is singular.
A singular subject in the present tense takes ‘is’.
Correct sentence: “Each of the applicants is required to submit a Personal Data Sheet.”

wrong.are: ‘Are’ is plural. The subject is ‘each’, which is singular; ‘applicants’ is not the subject.
wrong.were: ‘Were’ is plural (and past tense), but ‘each’ is singular.
wrong.have been: ‘Have’ is plural. A singular subject like ‘each’ would need ‘has been’.

3.tip: Each, every, either, neither, anyone, everyone = singular. Ignore the ‘of…’ phrase.

steps: Make a sentence with the first pair: “Books are kept and displayed in a library.”
Use the same sentence for the second pair: “Paintings are kept and displayed in a ____.”
The place where paintings are displayed is a gallery.

wrong.Artist: An artist makes paintings. This is a maker relationship, not a place where they are kept.
wrong.Canvas: Canvas is the material a painting is made on, not the place where it is displayed.
wrong.Frame: A frame holds one painting. A library holds many books, so the matching place is a gallery.

4.tip: Turn the first pair into a sentence, then test each choice in that same sentence.

steps: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the literal words.
Long ago, people used oil lamps at night. If you ‘burned the midnight oil’, you stayed awake late using the lamp.
Example: “Before the exam, Ana burned the midnight oil to review.” This means she studied late at night.

wrong.Waste resources: The idiom is not about wasting things; it is about staying up late to work or study.
wrong.Start a fire: This is a literal reading of ‘burn’. Idioms are not taken word for word.
wrong.Lose one’s temper: Losing your temper is about anger, which has nothing to do with working late.

5.tip: Midnight + oil lamp = working late at night.

steps: Look at the double letters in each choice.
The correct spelling has TWO c’s and TWO m’s: ac-com-mo-date.
Only ‘Accommodate’ has both doubles.

wrong.Acommodate: This has only one c. It needs two: ‘acc-’.
wrong.Accomodate: This has only one m. It needs two: ‘-comm-’.
wrong.Acomodate: This has only one c and one m. It needs two of each.

6.tip: Accommodate is big enough to ‘accommodate’ two c’s and two m’s.

steps: The subject is ‘She’, which is third-person singular (one person other than ‘I’ or ‘you’).
With he, she, or it, we use ‘does/doesn’t’, not ‘do/don’t’.
So part A, ‘don’t know’, is the error.
Correct sentence: “She doesn’t know the answer to the question asked earlier.”

wrong.B: ‘The answer’ is correct. It is the object of ‘know’ (the thing she does not know).
wrong.C: ‘To the question’ is correct. We say ‘the answer to a question’.
wrong.D: ‘Asked earlier’ is correct. It describes which question is meant.

steps: The subject is ‘The committee’. It is a collective noun, meaning one word that names a group.
Clue: the sentence says ‘its report’. ‘Its’ is singular, so the committee is acting as ONE unit.
A singular subject takes ‘has’.
Correct sentence: “The committee has already submitted its report.”

wrong.have: ‘Have’ is plural, but the committee acts as one group, as shown by ‘its’.
wrong.are: ‘Are’ is plural, and ‘are submitted’ would also wrongly make the committee the thing being submitted.
wrong.were: ‘Were’ is plural, and ‘were submitted’ would wrongly mean the committee itself was submitted.

8.tip: Group acting together (team, committee, family) + ‘its’ → singular verb.

steps: UBIQUITOUS means present or found everywhere.
Example: “Cellphones are ubiquitous; you see them in every jeepney, office and home.”
‘Present everywhere’ is exactly this meaning.

wrong.Rare: Rare means hard to find. That is the opposite of being everywhere.
wrong.Ancient: Ancient means very old. Ubiquitous is about place, not age.
wrong.Unclear: Unclear means hard to understand. It has no link to being found everywhere.

9.tip: Ubiquitous sounds like ‘you-bik-wi-tus’: you see it everywhere.

steps: The main idea is the one big point the whole passage makes.
The passage says public officials and employees must be ‘accountable to the people’.
It then lists high standards: ‘responsibility, integrity, competence, and loyalty’.
The choice that covers both parts is: public servants are accountable and must serve with high standards.

wrong.Public servants should be paid more: Pay or salary is never mentioned in the passage.
wrong.Only elected officials are accountable: The passage says ‘officials AND employees’, so it is not only elected officials.
wrong.Loyalty is owed to superiors only: Loyalty is one item in a list, and the passage says officials are accountable ‘to the people’, not only to superiors.

10.tip: The main idea must cover the WHOLE passage and must not add facts that are not there.

steps: Make a sentence with the first pair: “A doctor works in a hospital.”
Use the same sentence: “A teacher works in a ____.”
A teacher works in a school.

wrong.Student: A student is a person the teacher teaches, not the place where the teacher works.
wrong.Book: A book is a tool a teacher uses, not a workplace.
wrong.Lesson: A lesson is what a teacher gives, not where the teacher works.

11.tip: Worker : workplace. Keep the same relationship on both sides.

steps: The verb ‘has been working’ is present perfect continuous: an action that started in the past and is still going on.
‘2019’ is a starting point in time (a specific year), not a length of time.
Use ‘since’ for a starting point; use ‘for’ for a length of time (e.g., ‘for five years’).
Correct sentence: “He has been working in this office since 2019.”

wrong.for: ‘For’ goes with a length of time like ‘for six years’, not a starting point like 2019.
wrong.from: ‘From’ needs an end point (‘from 2019 to 2022’) and is not used this way with ‘has been working’.
wrong.during: ‘During’ means within a period (‘during 2019’), which would not show that he is still working now.

12.tip: SINCE + starting point (since Monday, since 2019). FOR + length (for 3 days, for 5 years).

steps: VERBOSE means using too many words.
Example: “His verbose speech lasted an hour but said very little.”
The opposite is ‘concise’, which means saying a lot in few words.

wrong.Wordy: Wordy means the same as verbose, so it is a synonym, not the opposite.
wrong.Loud: Loud is about volume, not the number of words.
wrong.Formal: Formal is about style or politeness, not about being long or short.

13.tip: Verbose = verb(al) overload. Opposite: concise, brief.

steps: ‘Between’ is a preposition, a word that shows a relationship (like to, for, with, between).
A pronoun after a preposition must be an object pronoun: me, him, her, us, them.
So it must be ‘between you and me’.
Test: remove ‘you and’. You would say ‘between… me’, never ‘between… I’.

‘I’ is a subject pronoun. After the preposition ‘between’ we need the object pronoun ‘me’.
wrong.Between you and myself, the plan will fa: ‘Myself’ is a reflexive pronoun; it is only used when ‘I’ already appears in the sentence (e.g., ‘I hurt myself’).
wrong.Between yourself and I, the plan will fa: This has two errors: ‘yourself’ should be ‘you’ and ‘I’ should be ‘me’.

14.tip: After a preposition (between, to, for, with): me, him, her, us, them.

steps: This sentence imagines something that is not true: I am not you.
For unreal or imagined situations in the present, English uses the subjunctive ‘were’ for ALL subjects (I were, he were, she were).
The second half ‘I would accept’ confirms it is an imagined situation.
Correct sentence: “If I were you, I would accept the offer.”

wrong.am: ‘Am’ states a real fact. You cannot actually be another person, so this is an unreal condition.
wrong.was: ‘Was’ is common in casual speech, but formal and exam English uses ‘were’ for imagined situations.
wrong.be: ‘Be’ is the base form and does not fit after ‘If I’ here.

15.tip: ‘If I were you…’: imagined situations always use ‘were’.

steps: MITIGATE means to make something less severe, painful, or serious.
Example: “Planting trees can mitigate the effects of flooding.”
‘Lessen’ means to make smaller or weaker, so it matches.

wrong.Worsen: Worsen means to make worse. That is the opposite of mitigate.
wrong.Ignore: Ignore means to pay no attention. Mitigate means to actively reduce a problem.
wrong.Repeat: Repeat means to do again. It has no connection to making something less serious.

steps: TRANSPARENT means light passes through it, so you can see through it (like clear glass).
The opposite is something light cannot pass through.
‘Opaque’ means not see-through, like a wooden door or a concrete wall.

wrong.Clear: Clear means see-through, which is the same as transparent.
wrong.Honest: Honest is a figurative meaning of transparent (an open process), so it is similar, not opposite.
wrong.Visible: Visible means can be seen. It is not the opposite of see-through.

17.tip: Transparent = see-through. Opaque = cannot see through.

steps: ‘Despite’ already means ‘even though there was’. It is never followed by ‘of’.
The phrase ‘in spite of’ uses ‘of’, which is why people mix them up.
So part A, ‘Despite of’, is the error.
Correct sentence: “Despite the heavy rain, the employees reported to work.”

wrong.B: ‘The heavy rain,’ is correct. It names what happened, and the comma correctly ends the opening phrase.
wrong.C: ‘The employees’ is correct. It is the subject of the sentence.
wrong.D: ‘Reported to work’ is correct. It is the verb in the past tense, matching the past event.

18.tip: Say ‘despite’ OR ‘in spite of’, never ‘despite of’.

steps: Make a sentence: “A pen is the tool a writer uses.”
Test: “A scalpel is the tool a ____ uses.”
A scalpel is a small, sharp knife used in operations, so the user is a surgeon.

wrong.Hospital: A hospital is a place, not the person who uses the scalpel.
wrong.Patient: The patient is the person operated on, not the one who uses the tool.
wrong.Blade: A blade is part of a scalpel, not the person who uses it.

19.tip: Tool : user. Ask, “Who uses this tool in their job?”

steps: Break the word: in- (not) + subordination (being under someone’s authority).
INSUBORDINATION means refusing to obey a superior’s lawful orders.
Example: “The clerk was charged with insubordination for refusing the director’s order.”

wrong.Lack of skill: That is incompetence or inefficiency, not refusing to obey.
wrong.Frequent absence: That is absenteeism or habitual absence, a different offense.
wrong.Dishonesty: Dishonesty is lying or cheating. Insubordination is about disobeying orders.

20.tip: Insubordination = not acting as a subordinate = disobeying the boss.

steps: This question asks what the passage SAYS, so look for the exact words.
The second sentence says: “It slows down services and increases the cost of transactions…”
That matches ‘Slows services and raises transaction costs’ word for word.

wrong.Protects the public from fraud: The passage never says red tape protects anyone; it describes red tape as a problem.
wrong.Applies only to private businesses: The passage says it affects ‘citizens and businesses’, not only businesses.
wrong.Is required by law: The passage calls red tape ‘excessive’ and ‘redundant’; it never says the law requires it.

21.tip: ‘According to the passage’ means the answer is written in the text. Find the matching words.

steps: Find the opening sentence. Sentence 2 starts with ‘First’ and names the person (Maria), so it comes first.
‘Next’ (sentence 4) comes after ‘First’: she filled it out.
‘Then’ (sentence 1): she submitted the form.
‘A week later’ (sentence 3): she got the interview call. Order: 2-4-1-3.

wrong.2-1-4-3: This has her submitting the form before filling it out, and ‘Next’ would come after ‘then’.
wrong.4-2-1-3: Sentence 4 says ‘Next’ and uses ‘it’, so it cannot be the opening sentence.
wrong.2-4-3-1: This puts the interview call before she submitted the form, which makes no sense.

22.tip: Follow the signal words: First → Next → Then → Later/Finally.

steps: Sentence 2 introduces ‘raw water’ being collected, so it is the first step.
Sentence 3 uses ‘It’ and ‘then’: the water is filtered and disinfected.
Sentence 4 says ‘The treated water’, which must come after it was treated: it is stored.
Sentence 1 has ‘Finally’, so it is last: water is piped to homes. Order: 2-3-4-1.

wrong.2-4-3-1: This stores the ‘treated’ water before it has been treated (filtered).
wrong.3-2-4-1: Sentence 3 starts with ‘It… then’, which refers back to something, so it cannot open the paragraph.
wrong.2-3-1-4: Sentence 1 says ‘Finally’, so it must be the last sentence, not third.

23.tip: Words like ‘it’, ‘then’ and ‘the treated…’ point back. ‘Finally’ always goes last.

steps: CANDID means honest and open; saying what you really think.
Example: “She gave a candid answer, even though the truth was hard to hear.”
‘Frank’ also means honest and direct, so it is the closest meaning.

wrong.Secretive: Secretive means hiding things. That is the opposite of candid.
wrong.Sweet: Sweet means nice or pleasant. Candid people can be blunt, not necessarily sweet.
wrong.Careful: Careful means cautious. A candid person speaks openly rather than carefully holding back.

24.tip: Candid = frank = straight to the point and honest.

steps: OBFUSCATE means to make something confusing or hard to understand on purpose.
Example: “The contract used technical terms to obfuscate the hidden fees.”
‘Make unclear’ is the same meaning.

wrong.Clarify: Clarify means to make clear. That is the opposite of obfuscate.
wrong.Decorate: Decorate means to make something look nice, not to make it confusing.
wrong.Delay: Delay is about time. Obfuscate is about making meaning unclear.

114.tip: Obfuscate sounds like ‘obscure’, both mean making things unclear.

steps: AMELIORATE means to make something better or improve it.
Example: “The new water system ameliorated living conditions in the barangay.”
The question asks for the OPPOSITE, so the answer is ‘worsen’.

wrong.Improve: Improve has the same meaning as ameliorate, so it is a synonym, not the opposite.
wrong.Praise: Praise means to say good things about someone. It is not related to making things better or worse.
wrong.Measure: Measure means to find the size or amount. It is not the opposite of improve.

115.tip: Ameliorate has ‘melior’, Latin for ‘better’. Its opposite is worsen.

steps: The subject is ‘The number’. ‘Of applicants’ only describes which number.
‘The number’ is a single amount (one figure), so it is singular.
A singular subject takes ‘has’.
Correct sentence: “The number of applicants has increased this year.”

wrong.have: ‘Have’ is plural, but the subject ‘the number’ is singular.
wrong.are: ‘Are’ is plural, and ‘are increased’ is not the usual way to say a number went up.
wrong.were: ‘Were’ is plural and past tense, and does not fit ‘this year’ or the singular subject.

116.tip: THE number of → singular (has). A number of → plural (have).

steps: ‘A number of’ means ‘several’ or ‘many’.
So the sentence really means “Several employees ___ on leave today,” and ‘employees’ is plural.
A plural subject in the present tense takes ‘are’.
Correct sentence: “A number of employees are on leave today.”

wrong.is: ‘Is’ is singular. ‘A number of’ means many, so the verb must be plural.
wrong.was: ‘Was’ is singular and past tense, but the sentence is about ‘today’ and many employees.
wrong.has been: ‘Has’ is singular. A plural subject would need ‘have been’.

117.tip: A number of = many → plural. The number of = one figure → singular.

steps: Make a sentence: “A prologue is the opening introduction of a novel.”
Test: “A preamble is the opening introduction of a ____.”
The best-known preamble is the opening part of the Constitution, so the answer is ‘Constitution’.

wrong.Law: Some laws have a preamble, but ‘law’ is too general; the classic pair is preamble : constitution.
wrong.Speech: A speech has an introduction, but it is not called a preamble.
wrong.Article: An article is a section inside the Constitution. The preamble comes before the articles.

118.tip: Intro : the work it introduces. Prologue → novel, preamble → constitution.

steps: The subject is ‘The report’, which is singular.
‘Along with the receipts’ is an extra phrase set off by commas. It does NOT make the subject plural.
A singular subject needs ‘was submitted’, not ‘were submitted’. So part B is the error.
Correct sentence: “The report, along with the receipts, was submitted to the accounting office yesterday.”

wrong.A: ‘Along with the receipts,’ is correct. It is an extra phrase that adds information.
wrong.C: ‘To the accounting’ is correct. ‘To’ shows where the report was sent.
wrong.D: ‘Office yesterday’ is correct. ‘Yesterday’ matches the past tense of the verb.

119.tip: Ignore phrases like ‘along with’, ‘as well as’, ‘together with’ when choosing the verb.

steps: ‘Who’ is a relative pronoun: it refers back to a noun before it.
Ask: who is always on time? Not just ‘she’, but ‘the employees’ (she is one of them).
‘Employees’ is plural, so ‘who’ is plural and takes ‘are’.
Correct sentence: “She is one of the employees who are always on time.”

wrong.is: ‘Is’ would make ‘who’ point to ‘she’ or ‘one’, but ‘who’ refers to the plural ‘employees’.
wrong.was: ‘Was’ is singular and past tense; ‘always on time’ describes a present habit of many employees.
wrong.has been: ‘Has been’ is singular; ‘who’ refers to the plural ‘employees’.

120.tip: In ‘one of the ___ who…’, the verb after ‘who’ matches the plural noun.

steps: PRUDENT means careful and showing good judgment, especially when making decisions.
Example: “It is prudent to save money for emergencies.”
‘Wise’ means showing good judgment, so it is the closest meaning.

wrong.Reckless: Reckless means careless about danger. That is the opposite of prudent.
wrong.Proud: Proud sounds a little like ‘prudent’ but means feeling pleased with yourself. The meanings are unrelated.
wrong.Quick: Quick is about speed. A prudent person thinks carefully, which is often slow.

steps: This is an idiom: its meaning is not literal.
‘To cut corners’ means to save time, effort or money by skipping steps, so the work becomes poor.
Example: “The contractor cut corners by using cheap cement, and the wall cracked.”

wrong.Take a shorter route: This is the literal picture of cutting a corner, but the idiom is about doing a job poorly.
wrong.Reduce staff: Cutting staff is a different idea (downsizing). The idiom is about doing work cheaply or carelessly.
wrong.Follow every rule: This is the opposite. Cutting corners means skipping rules or steps.

122.tip: Cutting corners = shortcuts that lower quality.

steps: Read the clue: ‘even first-time applicants understood them’. The blank must mean easy to understand.
LUCID means clear and easy to understand.
Correct sentence: “The new guidelines were so lucid that even first-time applicants understood them.”

wrong.vague: Vague means unclear. Unclear guidelines would NOT be easy for beginners to understand.
wrong.lengthy: Lengthy means long. Being long does not explain why beginners understood them.
wrong.obsolete: Obsolete means outdated. It does not explain why the guidelines were easy to understand.

123.tip: In ‘so ___ that…’ sentences, the ‘that’ part tells you the meaning of the blank.

steps: This asks what the passage says, so find the exact words.
The passage says appointments “shall be made only according to merit and fitness.”
That matches ‘Merit and fitness’ exactly.

wrong.Seniority and age: Seniority and age are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
wrong.Political endorsement: Political backing is not mentioned; the passage says ‘only’ merit and fitness.
wrong.Educational degree alone: The passage does not mention degrees, and ‘only according to merit and fitness’ rules this out.

124.tip: Pick the choice that repeats the passage’s key words, not one you assume is true.

steps: ‘Practicable’ means possible or able to be done.
‘As far as practicable’ means ‘whenever it is possible to do so’.
So exams are used when possible, but where an exam is not possible, a position may be filled another way.
This means some positions may be filled without a competitive exam.

wrong.All positions require an examination: If ALL positions required an exam, the writer would not need to add ‘as far as practicable’.
wrong.Examinations are optional for everyone: The phrase allows exceptions only when an exam is not possible; it does not make exams optional for all.
wrong.Only practical skills are tested: ‘Practicable’ (possible) is not the same as ‘practical skills’. The phrase is not about what is tested.

125.tip: ‘As far as practicable / possible’ = the rule applies, but with allowed exceptions.

steps: ‘By the time the director arrives’ points to a moment in the future.
We want an action that will be completed BEFORE that future moment.
That is the future perfect tense: will have + past participle.
Correct sentence: “By the time the director arrives, we will have finished the presentation.”

wrong.finish: ‘Finish’ is simple present and does not show the action will be done before the director arrives.
wrong.finished: ‘Finished’ is past tense, but the director’s arrival is in the future.
wrong.have finished: ‘Have finished’ is present perfect, which talks about now, not a point in the future.

126.tip: By the time + future event → will have + past participle.

steps: This asks for the MISSPELLED word, so three are correct and one is wrong.
Check each: occurrence (double c, double r), embarrass (double r, double s), maintenance — all correct.
The correct spelling is ‘liaison’ (li-ai-son). ‘Liaision’ adds an extra ‘i’, so it is misspelled.

wrong.Occurrence: This is spelled correctly: double c, double r, and ending in ‘-ence’.
wrong.Embarrass: This is spelled correctly: double r and double s.

127.tip: Liaison: two i’s around the a (l-I-A-I-son), then just ‘-son’.

steps: METICULOUS means paying very close attention to every detail.
Example: “The auditor was meticulous; she checked every receipt twice.”
‘Very careful’ means the same thing.

wrong.Careless: Careless means not paying attention. That is the opposite of meticulous.
wrong.Quick: Quick is about speed. Meticulous work is careful and often slow.
wrong.Generous: Generous means giving freely. It has nothing to do with attention to detail.

steps: SCARCE means in short supply; there is not enough of it.
Example: “Water is scarce during El Niño.”
The opposite is ‘abundant’, which means plentiful, more than enough.

wrong.Rare: Rare means hard to find. It is similar to scarce, not the opposite.
wrong.Small: Small is about size, not about how much of something is available.
wrong.Expensive: Scarce things are often expensive, but expensive is not the opposite of scarce.

199.tip: Scarce = too little. Abundant = a lot.

steps: The subject is ‘Every one’. ‘Of the forms’ only describes it.
‘Every one’ means each single one, so it is singular.
A singular subject takes ‘has’.
Correct sentence: “Every one of the forms has been signed.”

wrong.have: ‘Have’ is plural. The subject is ‘every one’ (singular), not ‘forms’.
wrong.were: ‘Were’ is plural, and ‘were been signed’ is not correct English.
wrong.are: ‘Are’ is plural, and ‘are been signed’ is not correct English.

200.tip: Every one / each one / any one of … → singular verb.

steps: Some verbs like suggest, recommend, insist and demand are followed by ‘that’ + the base form of the verb. This is called the subjunctive.
The base form is the simplest form of the verb, with no -s: submit, go, be.
So ‘she submits’ is wrong; it should be ‘she submit’. Part A is the error.
Correct sentence: “He suggested that she submit the documents before Friday.”

wrong.B: ‘The documents’ is correct. It is the object, the thing being submitted.
wrong.C: ‘Before’ is correct. It shows the deadline.
wrong.D: ‘Friday’ is correct. Days of the week are capitalized and need no article here.

201.tip: Suggest / recommend / insist that + base verb (no -s): ‘that she submit’.

steps: Make a sentence: “A famine is a serious lack of food.”
Test: “A drought is a serious lack of ____.”
A drought is a long period without enough rain, so it is a lack of water.

wrong.Farm: Farms are affected by drought, but a drought is not a lack of farms.
wrong.Heat: Droughts can come with heat, but a drought is not a lack of heat.
wrong.Desert: A desert is a dry place, not the thing that is missing during a drought.

202.tip: Shortage : what is missing. Famine → food, drought → water.

steps: An idiom’s meaning is not the same as its literal words.
‘In disguise’ means hidden or looking like something else. So a blessing in disguise is a good thing that first looked like a bad thing.
Example: “Failing the first exam was a blessing in disguise; I studied harder and passed with a high score.”

wrong.A hidden enemy: A blessing is something good, not an enemy.
wrong.A secret gift: The idiom is not about a secret present; it is about a bad event that turns out good.
wrong.A false promise: A false promise is something that disappoints. The idiom describes something that turns out well.

203.tip: Blessing in disguise = bad luck that turns out to be good luck.

steps: Count the people: ‘The two employees’, so exactly two.
Use ‘between’ for two people or things; use ‘among’ for three or more.
Correct sentence: “The two employees divided the work between themselves.”

wrong.among: ‘Among’ is for three or more. Here there are only two employees.
wrong.with: ‘Divided the work with themselves’ does not make sense; you divide something between people.
wrong.for: ‘For themselves’ means for their own benefit; it does not show the work was split between the two.

steps: Read the clue: the policy ‘was replaced with a new one’. So the blank must give a reason for replacing it.
OBSOLETE means outdated, no longer useful.
Correct sentence: “Because the policy was obsolete, it was replaced with a new one.”

wrong.popular: A popular policy is liked. That is not a reason to replace it.
wrong.recent: A recent policy is new. It makes no sense to replace it just because it is new.
wrong.effective: An effective policy works well. That is a reason to keep it, not replace it.

205.tip: ‘Because…’ sentences: the blank must logically cause the result.

steps: Look for what the passage says segregation does.
The second sentence says: “It reduces the volume sent to disposal facilities and makes recycling easier.”
That is ‘less waste for disposal and easier recycling’.

wrong.Lower garbage fees: Fees or costs are never mentioned in the passage.
wrong.More jobs in waste collection: Jobs are not mentioned in the passage.
wrong.Cleaner rivers: Rivers are not mentioned. This may be true in real life but it is not in the passage.

206.tip: Answer only from what the passage states, even if another choice sounds true in real life.

steps: DILIGENT means working hard and carefully, with steady effort.
Example: “The diligent student reviewed every night for the CSE.”
‘Hardworking’ is the closest meaning.

wrong.Lazy: Lazy means not wanting to work. That is the opposite of diligent.
wrong.Clever: Clever means smart. A person can be clever without working hard.
wrong.Polite: Polite means having good manners. It is not about effort in work.

steps: TERSE means using very few words; brief and to the point (sometimes a bit cold).
In the sentence, the manager gave a short reply to the complaint.
‘Brief’ is the closest meaning.

wrong.Rude: A terse reply can feel unfriendly, but terse mainly means short, not rude.
wrong.Detailed: Detailed means long and complete. That is the opposite of terse.
wrong.Late: Late is about time. Terse is about how short the reply is.

steps: The blank comes after ‘will’, so it needs a verb (an action word).
‘Affect’ is a verb meaning to influence or change something.
‘Effect’ is usually a noun meaning a result (‘the effect of the rule’).
Correct sentence: “The new rule will affect all employees.”

wrong.effect: ‘Effect’ is usually a noun (a result). As a verb it means ‘to bring about’, which does not fit here.
wrong.afect: This is a misspelling. The correct spelling is ‘affect’, with double f.
wrong.effects: ‘Effects’ is a plural noun (or ‘-s’ verb form). After ‘will’ we need the base verb ‘affect’.

steps: ‘To’ is a preposition, a word that shows a relationship like direction.
After a preposition, use an object pronoun: me, him, her, us, them.
Test: remove ‘the director and’. You would say ‘submit the report to me’, not ‘to I’.
Correct sentence: “Please submit the report to the director and me.”

wrong.I: ‘I’ is a subject pronoun. After the preposition ‘to’ we need ‘me’.
wrong.myself: ‘Myself’ is only used when ‘I’ is already the subject (‘I did it myself’). There is no ‘I’ in this sentence.
wrong.mine: ‘Mine’ shows ownership (‘the pen is mine’). You cannot submit a report ‘to mine’.

230.tip: Cover the other person: “to … me” sounds right, so keep “me”.

steps: Turn the question into a statement: “You did call ___ for the interview.”
The blank receives the action of ‘call’, so it is the object.
Answer it with a pronoun: “You called HIM.” ‘Him’ is an object pronoun, so use ‘whom’.
Correct sentence: “Whom did you call for the interview?”

wrong.Who: ‘Who’ is for the subject (the one doing the action). Here the person is the one being called, so ‘whom’ is correct in formal English.
wrong.Whose: ‘Whose’ shows ownership (‘Whose folder is this?’). It does not fit before ‘did you call’.
wrong.Whoever: ‘Whoever’ is not used to start a direct question like this.

231.tip: If the answer is ‘him’, use whom. If the answer is ‘he’, use who. (him/whom both end in m)

steps: ‘Lie’ means to rest or be in a flat position; it does NOT take an object.
‘Lay’ means to put something down; it NEEDS an object (‘lay the folders on the desk’).
The folders are just resting there; nobody is putting anything. So we need ‘lie’, whose -ing form is ‘lying’.
Correct sentence: “The folders have been lying on the desk since Monday.”

wrong.laying: ‘Laying’ comes from ‘lay’ (to put something down) and needs an object. The folders are not putting anything down.
wrong.laid: ‘Laid’ is the past form of ‘lay’. ‘Have been laid’ would mean someone put them there, and would not match ‘have been ___ing’.
wrong.lain: ‘Lain’ is the past participle of ‘lie’ (‘have lain’). After ‘have been’ we need the -ing form ‘lying’.

232.tip: Lie = rest (no object). Lay = put (needs an object).

steps: Choose ‘a’ or ‘an’ by the SOUND of the next word, not its first letter.
In ‘honest’ the h is silent, so it sounds like ‘on-est’, a vowel sound.
Use ‘an’ before a vowel sound.
Correct sentence: “She is an honest employee.”

wrong.a: ‘A’ is used before a consonant sound. ‘Honest’ starts with a vowel sound because the h is silent.
wrong.the: ‘The’ points to a specific, already known employee. The sentence is describing her as one honest employee in general.
wrong.no article needed: A singular countable noun like ‘employee’ needs an article. ‘She is honest employee’ is incorrect.

233.tip: an hour, an honest man, a house, a university: listen to the sound.

steps: The subject is ‘Neither’. ‘Of the reports’ only describes it.
‘Neither’ used alone means ‘not one and not the other’. It is treated as singular.
A singular subject takes ‘is’.
Correct sentence: “Neither of the reports is complete.”

wrong.are: ‘Are’ is plural, but ‘neither’ is singular. ‘Reports’ is not the subject.
wrong.were: ‘Were’ is plural, and it changes the tense to past.
wrong.have been: ‘Have’ is plural. A singular subject would need ‘has been’.

234.tip: Neither of / either of / each of + plural noun → singular verb.

steps: Two people are compared: Ramon and his brother. Comparing two uses the comparative form.
For short words like ‘tall’, the comparative adds -er: taller.
Never use ‘more’ and ‘-er’ together.
Correct sentence: “Ramon is taller than his brother.”

wrong.more taller: This is a double comparative. ‘Taller’ already means ‘more tall’, so ‘more’ is extra.
wrong.tallest: ‘Tallest’ is the superlative, used for three or more. Here only two people are compared, and ‘than’ needs a comparative.
wrong.most tall: ‘Most’ is for superlatives (three or more), and short words like ‘tall’ use -est, not ‘most’.

235.tip: Two things + ‘than’ → -er (or ‘more’ for long words), never both.

steps: Count the items: ‘Of the three proposals’, so three are compared.
When comparing three or more, use the superlative form.
The superlative of ‘good’ is ‘best’ (good → better → best).
Correct sentence: “Of the three proposals, this one is the best.”

wrong.better: ‘Better’ is comparative, used for only two things. There are three proposals.
wrong.good: ‘Good’ alone does not compare. ‘The good’ also sounds wrong after ‘of the three’.
wrong.more good: This is not standard English. ‘Good’ has special forms: better and best.

steps: This sentence talks about the PAST and something that did not happen: I did not know, so I did not attend.
This is a past unreal condition (third conditional).
Pattern: If + had + past participle, … would have + past participle.
Correct sentence: “I would have attended the meeting if I had known about it.”

wrong.knew: ‘If I knew’ is for imagined situations in the present, not the past.
wrong.know: ‘If I know’ is for real, possible situations, not for something that did not happen in the past.
wrong.would know: ‘Would’ is not used in the if-part of a conditional sentence.

237.tip: Would have … if … had: both halves use ‘have/had’ for the unreal past.

steps: A lobby is an enclosed space, a room with walls.
Use ‘in’ for being inside an enclosed space (in a room, in the lobby, in the car).
Correct sentence: “The applicants were told to wait in the lobby.”

wrong.at: ‘At’ is for a point or general location (‘at the door’, ‘at the office’). Since the people are inside the lobby, ‘in’ fits better.
wrong.on: ‘On’ is for surfaces (‘on the desk’, ‘on the floor’), not inside a room.
wrong.into: ‘Into’ shows movement toward the inside (‘walk into the lobby’). Waiting is not movement.

238.tip: IN = inside a space. ON = on a surface. AT = at a point. INTO = moving inside.

steps: The subject is ‘Each’, which is singular. ‘Of the clerks’ only describes it.
A singular subject takes ‘has’, not ‘have’. So part B, ‘have their own’, is the error.
Formal English also uses ‘his or her own’ to match the singular ‘each’.
Correct sentence: “Each of the clerks has his or her own assigned workstation.”

wrong.A: ‘Each of the clerks’ is correct. It is the subject phrase.
wrong.C: ‘Assigned’ is correct. It describes the workstation.
wrong.D: ‘Workstation’ is correct. It is singular because each clerk has one.

239.tip: Each = one at a time → has, not have.

steps: The subject is ‘The director’, which is singular.
‘As well as her assistants’ is an extra phrase between commas. It does not change the subject.
A singular subject needs ‘is attending’, not ‘are attending’. So part B is the error.
Correct sentence: “The director, as well as her assistants, is attending the conference in Cebu.”

wrong.A: ‘As well as her assistants,’ is correct. It is an extra phrase set off by commas.
wrong.C: ‘The conference’ is correct. It tells what she is attending.
wrong.D: ‘In Cebu’ is correct. ‘In’ is used for cities.

240.tip: ‘As well as’, ‘along with’, ‘together with’ do not make the subject plural.

steps: Check the c’s and the s’s.
The correct spelling has ONE c and TWO s’s: ne-ces-sa-ry.
Only ‘Necessary’ has this pattern.

wrong.Neccessary: This has two c’s. It needs only one c.
wrong.Necesary: This has only one s. It needs two s’s.
wrong.Neccesary: This has two c’s and one s, which is the reverse of the correct pattern.

241.tip: Necessary: one Collar, two Sleeves (1 c, 2 s).

steps: Start from ‘question’ and add ‘-naire’.
The correct spelling has a double n: question + n + aire = questionnaire.
Only ‘Questionnaire’ has the double n, ‘-aire’ ending, and the ‘s’ in ‘ques’.

wrong.Questionaire: This has only one n. It needs two: ‘questio-nn-aire’.
wrong.Questionnare: This is missing the ‘i’ in the ending. It should be ‘-naire’.

steps: Look for the letters after ‘priv’ and before the ending.
The correct spelling is p-r-i-v-i-l-e-g-e: ‘i’ after the v, ‘e’ after the l, and no d.
Only ‘Privilege’ follows this.

wrong.Priviledge: This has an extra d. Privilege does not end in ‘-ledge’.
wrong.Privelege: This has an e after the v. It should be an i: ‘privi-’.
wrong.Privilage: This has an a after the l. It should be an e: ‘-lege’.

243.tip: Privilege has no ‘ledge’ in it: privi + lege.

steps: ADAMANT means refusing to change your mind; very firm.
In the sentence, the supervisor would not move or extend the deadline.
‘Firm and unyielding’ (not giving in) is the same meaning.

wrong.Unsure: Unsure means not certain. An adamant person is very certain.
wrong.Angry: An adamant person may be calm; adamant is about being firm, not about anger.
wrong.Careless: Careless means not paying attention. Being firm about a deadline shows the opposite.

244.tip: Adamant sounds like ‘diamond’, hard and unbreakable.

steps: CONCEDE means to admit that something is true, or to give in.
Example: “After the count, the candidate conceded defeat.”
The question asks for the OPPOSITE. Refusing to admit something is to ‘deny’ it.

wrong.Admit: Admit has the same meaning as concede, so it is a synonym.
wrong.Yield: Yield means to give in, which is also a meaning of concede.
wrong.Accept: Accept is close to concede (accepting a loss), not the opposite.

steps: PERUSE means to read something carefully and thoroughly.
Example: “Peruse the contract before you sign it.”
‘Read carefully’ is the same meaning.

wrong.Ignore: Ignore means to pay no attention. Perusing means paying close attention.
wrong.Pursue: Pursue (to chase or follow) only looks similar in spelling. It has a different meaning.
wrong.Publish: Publish means to print and release a text, not to read it.

246.tip: Peruse = pore over a document (study it closely).

steps: INEVITABLE means certain to happen; it cannot be stopped or avoided.
Example: “With heavy rain all week, flooding in the low areas was inevitable.”
‘Unavoidable’ means the same thing.

wrong.Unlikely: Unlikely means probably will not happen. Inevitable means it surely will.
wrong.Invisible: Invisible means cannot be seen. It only starts with the same ‘in-’.
wrong.Uncertain: Uncertain means not sure. Inevitable means completely sure to happen.

steps: EXONERATE means to officially clear someone of blame or guilt.
Example: “New evidence exonerated the employee, so the charges were dropped.”
The opposite is to blame or charge someone, which is ‘accuse’.

wrong.Free: To exonerate frees someone from blame, so ‘free’ is similar, not opposite.
wrong.Forgive: Forgive is close in feeling (letting go of blame), not the opposite.
wrong.Release: Release is similar to free, which is close to exonerate, not opposite.

248.tip: Exonerate = ex (out of) + onus (burden): taking the blame off. Opposite: accuse.

steps: PROFICIENT means good at something because of skill and practice.
Example: “She is proficient in Excel and can make reports quickly.”
‘Skilled’ is the closest meaning.

wrong.Proud: Proud only starts with ‘pro-’ like proficient. It means pleased with yourself, not skilled.
wrong.Productive: Productive means producing a lot. You can be productive without being highly skilled.
wrong.Professional: Professional refers to a job or behavior suitable for work. It does not exactly mean skilled.

249.tip: Do not be fooled by words that only look alike (pro-). Focus on meaning.

steps: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not literal.
Hitting a nail exactly on its head drives it in perfectly. So the idiom means to say something exactly right, especially about the cause of a problem.
Example: “When she said poor planning caused the delay, she hit the nail on the head.”

wrong.Hurt oneself: This is a literal picture of hammering badly, not the idiom’s meaning.
wrong.Work as a carpenter: This takes the hammer-and-nail image literally. The idiom is about being exactly right.
wrong.Make a mistake: This is the opposite. Hitting the nail on the head means being exactly correct.

250.tip: Hit the nail on the head = exactly right.

steps: This idiom is not about real beans.
‘To spill the beans’ means to tell a secret, often by accident or too early.
Example: “Someone spilled the beans about the surprise party for our boss.”

wrong.Waste food: This is the literal picture of spilling beans, not the idiom’s meaning.
wrong.Make a mess: Spilling can make a mess literally, but the idiom means revealing a secret.
wrong.Start a quarrel: Starting a fight is a different idea. The idiom is about letting out secret information.

251.tip: Spill the beans = let the secret out.

steps: A ‘blue moon’ is an extra full moon that happens only about once every two to three years.
So ‘once in a blue moon’ means very rarely.
Example: “My cousin from abroad visits only once in a blue moon.”

wrong.Every month: A full moon happens every month, but a ‘blue moon’ is rare. The idiom means rarely, not monthly.
wrong.At night: The idiom is about how often, not about what time of day.
wrong.Never: Rarely still means it happens sometimes. ‘Never’ means not at all.

252.tip: Once in a blue moon = rarely, but not never.

steps: Long ago, soldiers bit on a bullet to bear pain during surgery without medicine.
So ‘to bite the bullet’ means to face something unpleasant or difficult with courage.
Example: “He bit the bullet and told his boss about the mistake.”

wrong.Get hurt: The idiom is not about getting injured; it is about bravely accepting something hard.
wrong.Eat quickly: This is a literal reading of ‘bite’. The idiom is not about eating.
wrong.Avoid responsibility: This is the opposite. Biting the bullet means facing the problem, not running from it.

253.tip: Bite the bullet = just face it bravely.

steps: A wet blanket is used to put out a fire.
So a person who is ‘a wet blanket’ ‘puts out’ the fun or excitement of others.
Example: “Don’t be a wet blanket; join us at the party!”

wrong.Is always crying: ‘Wet’ here does not mean tears. The idiom is about ruining others’ fun.
wrong.Works very hard: Hard work is not part of the meaning. A wet blanket kills the mood.
wrong.Is easily fooled: A person easily fooled is ‘gullible’ or ‘naive’, which is a different idea.

254.tip: Wet blanket puts out the fire = kills the fun.

steps: Hunters once beat bushes to scare out animals instead of going straight for them.
So ‘to beat around the bush’ means to avoid saying something directly.
Example: “Stop beating around the bush and tell me if I passed.”

wrong.Work in a garden: This is the literal picture of bushes, not the idiom’s meaning.
wrong.Win a contest: ‘Beat’ here does not mean defeat someone. It is about avoiding the main point.
wrong.Search carefully: Searching carefully is about looking for something. The idiom is about not speaking directly.

255.tip: Beat around the bush = not getting to the point.

steps: Make a sentence: “Hot is the opposite of cold.”
Test: “Ascend is the opposite of ____.”
Ascend means to go up, so the opposite is ‘descend’, to go down.

wrong.Climb: Climb means to go up, which is similar to ascend, not the opposite.
wrong.Rise: Rise also means to go up. It is a synonym of ascend.
wrong.Mountain: A mountain is a thing you might ascend, not the opposite of ascend.

256.tip: Check if the first pair are opposites, synonyms, or something else, then match it.

steps: Make a sentence: “An author creates a novel.”
Test: “A composer creates a ____.”
A composer writes music, so the answer is ‘Song’.

wrong.Piano: A piano is an instrument a composer may use, not the work the composer creates.
wrong.Orchestra: An orchestra performs music. It is a group of musicians, not the creation.
wrong.Singer: A singer performs songs. The composer creates them.

257.tip: Creator : creation. Author → novel, composer → song.

steps: Make a sentence: “Minutes make up an hour” (60 minutes = 1 hour).
Test: “Months make up a ____.”
12 months make up a year.

wrong.Week: A week is smaller than a month, so months do not make up a week.
wrong.Day: A day is smaller than a month, so the order is reversed.
wrong.Calendar: A calendar is a chart that shows time, not a unit of time.

258.tip: Small unit : the bigger unit it builds. Keep the same direction.

steps: Make a sentence: “A carpenter uses a saw as a tool.”
Test: “A tailor uses a ____ as a tool.”
A tailor sews clothes with a needle.

wrong.Cloth: Cloth is the material a tailor works on, not the tool. (A carpenter’s material would be wood.)
wrong.Shirt: A shirt is the product a tailor makes, not the tool.
wrong.Shop: A shop is the workplace, not the tool.

259.tip: Worker : tool. Do not confuse tool with material, product or place.

steps: Make a sentence: “Bricks are put together to build a wall.”
Test: “Letters are put together to build a ____.”
Letters are combined to form a word.

wrong.Pen: A pen is a tool for writing letters. It is not made of letters.
wrong.Mail: ‘Letter’ here means a letter of the alphabet, not a mailed letter. This choice uses the wrong meaning.
wrong.Alphabet: The alphabet is the full list of letters, not something you build by putting letters together like bricks.

260.tip: Part : whole that is built from it. Watch out for words with two meanings.

steps: Sentence 2 introduces the topic (the agency launched an online appointment system), so it opens.
Sentence 3 explains how it works: applicants choose a time slot.
Sentence 1 starts with ‘As a result’, so it must come after the cause: the queue got shorter.
Sentence 4 talks about ‘next year’, the future plan, so it comes last. Order: 2-3-1-4.

wrong.2-1-3-4: This gives the result before explaining how the system works. The explanation (3) should come before the result.
wrong.3-2-1-4: Sentence 3 says ‘now’ about a system that has not been introduced yet, so it cannot open the paragraph.
wrong.2-3-4-1: This puts the result (1) after the future plan, separating ‘As a result’ from its cause.

261.tip: Action → explanation → result (‘As a result’) → future plan.

steps: Sentence 2 introduces the topic: the town planned a new bridge. It opens the paragraph.
Sentence 4 tells when work started: January.
Sentence 1 begins with ‘However’, which shows a problem against the plan: rain delays.
Sentence 3 says ‘finally’ opened in September, so it is last. Order: 2-4-1-3.

wrong.4-2-1-3: This puts the start of construction before the bridge is introduced, so we would not know what was being built.
wrong.2-1-4-3: This says the work was delayed before construction even began.
wrong.4-1-2-3: This starts with construction and the delay before introducing the bridge and the plan.

steps: A good opening sentence must make sense alone; it cannot point back to something before it.
Look for words that refer back: ‘For this reason’ (A), ‘These files’ (C), ‘then’ (D).
Sentence B states a general problem with no back-reference: paper records take space and get damaged.
So B is the best opening sentence.

wrong.A: ‘For this reason’ refers to a reason given earlier, so A must come after another sentence.
wrong.C: ‘These files’ refers to files already mentioned, so C cannot be first.
wrong.D: ‘Then’ shows a step after something else happened, so D cannot be first.

263.tip: Words like this, these, then, however, as a result usually cannot start a paragraph.

steps: This is a NOT question: find the item the passage does NOT list.
The passage lists: procedure, person responsible, maximum time, fees, and documents needed.
Salary of the employee is not in that list.

wrong.The fees to be paid: Fees are mentioned: “…the fees, and the documents needed.”
wrong.The maximum time for each step: Time is mentioned: “…the maximum time it takes…”
wrong.The documents needed: Documents are mentioned: “…and the documents needed.”

264.tip: For NOT questions, cross out each choice you can find in the passage.

steps: This asks where the Charter must be posted, so look for a place.
The last sentence says: “Offices must post it in a visible place and on their website.”
That matches ‘In a visible place and on the office website’.

wrong.Only in the head office: The passage does not mention a head office, and it says the website too, not ‘only’ one place.
wrong.Only in newspapers: Newspapers are not mentioned in the passage.
wrong.In the mayor’s office: The mayor’s office is not mentioned. Every office must post its own Charter.

265.tip: Be careful with ‘only’ in choices; it often makes them wrong.

steps: Use context clues: the passage is about ‘the variety of life on Earth’ (biodiversity).
‘Mega-’ means very large or many; ‘diverse’ means varied.
So a megadiverse country has a very large variety of living things.

wrong.Having very large animals: ‘Mega’ here describes the amount of variety, not the size of animals.
wrong.Having many islands: The Philippines has many islands, but the passage is about variety of life, not geography.
wrong.Having polluted habitats: Pollution is mentioned as a threat, not as the meaning of megadiverse.

266.tip: Break the word into parts (mega + diverse) and check it against the passage’s topic.

steps: This is a NOT question: find the threat the passage does not name.
The passage lists the threats: “habitat loss, pollution and over-harvesting.”
Typhoons are not in that list.

wrong.Habitat loss: Habitat loss is named in the passage as a threat.
wrong.Pollution: Pollution is named in the passage as a threat.
wrong.Over-harvesting: Over-harvesting is named in the passage as a threat.

267.tip: For NOT questions, the answer is the one thing missing from the passage’s list.

steps: Sentence 1 states a claim: raising the minimum wage causes job losses.
Sentence 2 starts with ‘Yet’, a signal word for contrast, and gives evidence against the claim: little or no job loss from moderate increases.
So the author’s purpose is to question (challenge) that claim.

wrong.Argue that every wage increase is harmfu: The author gives evidence that moderate increases did NOT hurt jobs, which is the opposite.
wrong.Explain how wages are computed: The passage does not explain any computation of wages.
wrong.Describe how to apply for a job: Job applications are not discussed at all.

268.tip: ‘Some say… Yet…’ means the author is challenging what ‘some say’.
